books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address, March 4, 1865. Public domain. Wording verified against the Avalon Project and National Park Service texts. “. . .” marks omitted text between passages, quoted in their order in the source.
stimulus.text:
“One-eighth of the whole population were colored slaves, not distributed generally over the Union, but localized in the southern part of it. These slaves constituted a peculiar and powerful interest. All knew that this interest was somehow the cause of the war. . . . Yet, if God wills that it continue, until all the wealth piled by the bond-man’s 250 years of unrequited toil shall be sunk, and until every drop of blood drawn with the lash, shall be paid by another drawn with the sword, as was said 3,000 years ago, so still it must be said ‘the judgments of the Lord, are true and righteous altogether.’ . . . With malice toward none; with charity for all; . . . let us strive on to finish the work we are in; to bind up the nation’s wounds.”

—Abraham Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address, March 4, 1865

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Lincoln delivered this address on March 4, 1865. The war’s end a month later left one part of his vision unfinished: slavery still existed in the loyal border states. That gap was closed by

options.text: the Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in December 1865.
the Emancipation Proclamation, issued in January 1863.
options.misconception: Background: the Emancipation Proclamation freed people only in rebel territory and left slavery in the border states untouched.

options.text: the Gettysburg Address, delivered in November 1863.
options.misconception: Background: the Gettysburg Address was a speech rededicating the war to equality; it freed no one.
Background: the Confiscation Acts seized rebel property and slave labor used for the rebellion; they did not end slavery in the border states.

rationales.B: Background: the Emancipation Proclamation freed people only in rebel territory and left slavery in the border states untouched.
rationales.C: Background: the Gettysburg Address was a speech rededicating the war to equality; it freed no one.
rationales.D: Background: the Confiscation Acts seized rebel property and slave labor used for the rebellion; they did not end slavery in the border states.
rationales.A: The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in December 1865, banned slavery everywhere in the country, including the border states the proclamation had left out.
rationales.general:
1. The address is March 1865, and the war ends in April.
2. Victory frees the rebel states, but the border states still hold enslaved people.
3. A wartime order cannot finish the job; only the Constitution can.
4. Background: the Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in December 1865, bans slavery everywhere.
Remember: a proclamation frees where it reaches, and an amendment finishes what it leaves behind.
